title: The Clock of Manchester's mill district
premise: In 1918, Yara Vasquez drives suffragist Edith Marlowe through Manchester's mill district, reading her correspondence before delivery as a matter of habit and quiet loyalty. One sealed letter reveals that the Hargreave family — mill owners bankrolling the suffrage cause — are orchestrating a false flag sabotage meant to crush a strike and discredit the movement itself. When Edith is silenced by an 'accident,' Yara inherits both her letters and her unfinished fight, carrying the evidence through three checkpoints controlled by police, soldiers, and the Hargreaves' own men before the armistice celebrations drown all truth in confetti. He reaches a sympathetic journalist at the eleventh hour; the story breaks days after the armistice, the Hargreaves' empire cracks, and Yara — once certain history happened to other people — signs his own name to the testimony.
about_author: Petra Dunmore is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing industrial-era correspondence in northern England, where she first encountered letters never meant for history's eyes. She writes historical fiction about the people who carried messages rather than made them.

chapters.title: The Route Through Ancoats
chapters.summary: Yara Vasquez, driver and unofficial reader of Edith Marlowe's post, navigates the mill district on a grey November morning, establishing his routines, his outsider status as a Spanish immigrant's son, and his belief that history happens elsewhere. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: comfortable invisibility about to be broken.

chapters.title: Letters Worth Stealing
chapters.summary: Yara reads the day's correspondence: strike notices, threats, donations. Edith catches him lingering over one letter but instead of anger, she tests him with a question about justice. Their wary alliance deepens. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: belonging offered cautiously.

chapters.title: The Hargreave Subscription
chapters.summary: At a fundraising dinner, Yara observes the Hargreave family's lavish patronage of the suffrage cause and the unease it provokes among working women. A mill girl, Bess Whitaker, warns him that generosity has a price. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: first crack in his assumptions.

chapters.title: Sealed in Wax
chapters.summary: A letter arrives sealed twice over, addressed not to Edith but to 'the carrier.' Inside: dates, a warehouse, and the Hargreave name beside a plan for staged sabotage. Yara must decide whether to deliver it or keep it. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: dread and complicity.

chapters.title: What Edith Already Knew
chapters.summary: Yara confronts Edith; she admits suspicions but lacks proof and fears destroying the movement by scandal. She instructs him to forget it. He cannot. POV: alternating Yara and Edith. Emotional beat: loyalty strained against conscience.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Police Station Steps
chapters.summary: Yara tests the waters by approaching a sympathetic constable, Sergeant Doyle, and is warned off — politely, then less so. He realizes the law is already bought. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: the law fails him.

chapters.title: Bess of the Bobbin Floor
chapters.summary: Yara seeks out Bess Whitaker inside Hargreave Mill No. 3, where she shows him the locked bay the letter described. Workers whisper about 'the night work' no one is paid for. POV: Bess. Emotional beat: solidarity across class lines.

chapters.title: The Accident on London Road
chapters.summary: Edith's motor is forced off the road; she dies before the ambulance arrives. The inquest rules misadventure within hours. Yara, who was meant to be driving, understands the message intended for him. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into resolve.

chapters.title: Inheritance of Paper
chapters.summary: Sorting Edith's effects, Yara finds her private dossier corroborating the letter — and a note naming him as her courier if anything happened. Now he carries evidence three parties will kill for. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance.

chapters.title: Men in Good Coats
chapters.summary: Hargreave's fixer, Mr. Calloway, visits Yara with an offer: money, passage to Spain, silence. Yara plays dull and agrees to think it over, buying time while learning how far the family's reach extends. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: fear managed as performance.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Goods Yard
chapters.summary: Yara attempts to move the dossier out of the district via a railway contact; soldiers enforcing wartime security nearly find it hidden in a spare tyre. Bess covers for him at cost to herself. POV: alternating Yara and Bess. Emotional beat: trust tested under searchlights.

chapters.title: The Strike Turns Ugly
chapters.summary: The staged sabotage begins early: a fire at the canal depot, blamed on strikers. Two men are arrested; one is Bess's brother. The district seethes, and Yara sees the plot working exactly as designed. POV: Bess. Emotional beat: rage sharpening purpose.

chapters.title: Doyle's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Sergeant Doyle, sickened by the frame-up, secretly passes Yara the patrol schedule — the locations of all three checkpoints — but refuses to go further. Justice outside the law now has a map. POV: Doyle. Emotional beat: conscience splitting from uniform.

chapters.title: Calloway's Second Visit
chapters.summary: Calloway returns, no longer offering money. He knows about Bess, about the goods yard, about everything except where the papers are. Yara gives up nothing but learns the deadline: the armistice, expected within days. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: terror converted to clarity.

chapters.title: The Journalist in the Attic
chapters.summary: Edith's dossier names a reporter, Nathaniel Okafor of the Manchester Evening Chronicle, who once printed what others wouldn't. Yara finds him hiding after his office was raided. They agree: the story must run the day the armistice does. POV: Okafor. Emotional beat: hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Bridge at Beswick
chapters.summary: The final route crosses the canal bridge where Hargreave's men wait. Yara splits the evidence — copies with Bess via the mill girls' laundry cart, originals on himself — and walks into the trap deliberately. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen, not suffered.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Gaslight
chapters.summary: Calloway interrogates Yara in the mill office while the town waits for armistice news. Yara stalls, lies, and endures, betting that Calloway cannot risk killing him before knowing where the originals are. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: endurance as resistance.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Hour
chapters.summary: As church bells announce the armistice, Bess and the laundry cart arrive; in the chaos of celebration crowds flooding past the mill, she frees Yara. Calloway pursues into streets gone mad with joy. POV: Bess. Emotional beat: liberation amid jubilation.

chapters.title: Confetti and Ink
chapters.summary: Okafor's special edition hits the streets between the armistice bulletins: the Hargreave plot, the forged evidence, Edith's death re-examined. Crowds read truth amid celebration. The family's allies scatter. POV: Okafor. Emotional beat: vindication, bittersweet.

chapters.title: The Reckoning That Isn't
chapters.summary: Old Hargreave dies conveniently before charges land; Calloway vanishes; the courts take the fall of underlings. Yara rages at justice half-served until Bess reminds him what actually changed: the workers now know, and knowledge doesn't die quietly. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: disillusion tempered by hard-won meaning.

chapters.title: Mill No. 3, Reopened
chapters.summary: Months later, the mill reopens under new management with the union recognized; Bess stands on the bobbin floor as a steward. Yara takes honest work driving again — but for the union now. POV: Bess. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Signed in His Own Hand
chapters.summary: At the public inquiry's final session, Yara delivers his testimony and, when asked his name for the record, gives it fully — no longer a man history happens around, but one who signed himself into it. The last letter he reads is his own statement. POV: Yara. Emotional beat: arrival; history is his address now.
